content: 1. Historical data from the smallpox eradication era suggests that individuals receiving their primary vaccination were the main source of vaccinia virus transmission to their contacts. This is likely due to their higher or prolonged viral shedding compared to those who were revaccinated. 2. Transmission of the vaccinia virus typically required close personal interaction, most commonly occurring within households and often involving children. 3. Nosocomial transmission of vaccinia virus from patients or healthcare workers to other patients has been rarely documented. In most cases, the source of the virus was a patient experiencing an adverse reaction following vaccination. 4. The majority of vaccinia virus transmission cases involved direct person-to-person contact. However, in some instances, the exact mode of transmission could not be determined. 5. Secondary transmission of the vaccinia virus is infrequent, particularly from adults, and requires close contact. 6. In the present day, the risk of vaccinia virus transmission and the potential for serious adverse events following transmission may be higher than during the smallpox eradication era. 7. During earlier studies, most healthcare workers had been previously vaccinated, reducing their likelihood of transmitting vaccinia. Additionally, most patients were also vaccinated, making them less susceptible to infection. 8. The exact number of healthcare workers vaccinated during earlier study periods is unknown, but vaccination of healthcare workers was routinely recommended at the time. 9. Currently, the number of hospitalized patients at risk for serious complications from vaccinia infection is higher. This includes individuals with compromised immune systems due to HIV/AIDS, chemotherapy, immunosuppressive medications, organ transplantation, or similar conditions. 10. More patients with indwelling invasive devices, such as intravenous lines, arterial lines, dialysis equipment, ostomies, or central venous lines, are now being cared for in hospital settings. 11. Infection control practices have improved significantly, and healthcare workers are now more aware of these practices compared to earlier years. 12. New approaches to vaccination site care, such as the use of semipermeable dressings, provide an effective barrier to contain the vaccinia virus. 13. Optimal infection control practices, as recommended by ACIP and HICPAC, should effectively eliminate the risk of vaccinated healthcare workers transmitting vaccinia to patients. Requiring administrative leave for vaccinated workers could lead to staffing shortages, potentially posing risks to patient care. 14. Healthcare personnel providing direct patient care after smallpox vaccination should keep their vaccination sites covered with gauze or similar absorbent material combined with a semipermeable dressing. This helps absorb exudates and provides a barrier to minimize the risk of virus transmission. 15. Products combining an absorbent base with an overlying semipermeable layer can also be used to cover the vaccination site. 16. Semipermeable dressings are effective barriers to the vaccinia virus. However, using them alone can lead to maceration of the vaccination site, increased irritation, and itching, which may result in touching, scratching, and potential contamination of the hands. 17. During direct patient care, the vaccination site should be covered with gauze, a semipermeable dressing, and a layer of clothing until the scab separates. 18. Dressings covering the vaccination site should be changed frequently, approximately every 3-5 days or more often if exudates accumulate, to prevent maceration. 19. This should be performed after any contact with the vaccination site or materials that have come into contact with the site and before patient contact. 20. Care should be taken to avoid contact with the vaccination site or contaminated materials from the site. 21. Hospitals should include a vaccination site-care component in their smallpox vaccination programs. Designated staff should assess the dressings of vaccinated healthcare workers daily, determine if dressings need changing, and change them if necessary. 22. Designated staff should also assess the vaccination site for local reactions and vaccine take, reinforce the importance of meticulous hand hygiene to vaccinees, and record and report any serious adverse events following vaccination. 23. When feasible, staff responsible for dressing changes should be vaccinated. However, it is acceptable for non-vaccinated staff to perform dressing changes if necessary. 24. All individuals handling bandages should observe contact precautions. 25. Individuals outside the patient-care setting, such as public health response team members not involved in patient care or healthcare workers not at work, can keep their vaccination sites covered with a porous dressing (e.g., gauze). Hand hygiene remains critical in preventing inadvertent inoculation. 26. In non-patient-care settings where vaccinia transmission is a concern due to close personal contact with children or others, the vaccination site should be covered with gauze or similar absorbent material and clothing. 27. Hypoallergenic tape should be used for individuals with tape hypersensitivity. 28. The vaccination site should be kept dry, although normal showering or bathing can continue. 29. A waterproof dressing may reduce the risk of autoinoculation while washing. If the site is uncovered, care should be taken to avoid touching it. 30. After showering, if the vaccination site is wet, it should be blotted dry with gauze, which should then be discarded. 31. If a towel is used to dry the site, it should not be used to dry the rest of the body. 32. Alternatively, the site can be allowed to air dry before replacing the bandage. 33. No salves, creams, or ointments should be applied to the vaccination site. 34. Contaminated bandages and, if possible, the vaccination site scab (after it has fallen off) should be placed in sealed plastic bags before disposal in the trash to reduce the potential for inadvertent transmission of the live virus. 35. Clothing, towels, and other cloth materials that have come into contact with the site can be decontaminated through routine laundering in hot water. 36. FDA guidance on smallpox vaccination and related precautions is available online. 37. Administrative leave is not routinely required for newly vaccinated healthcare personnel unless they are physically unable to work due to systemic signs and symptoms of illness, have extensive skin lesions that cannot be adequately covered, or are unable to adhere to recommended infection-control precautions. 38. The close contact required for vaccinia transmission to household contacts is unlikely to occur in the healthcare setting. 39. The FDA recommends that vaccinees defer blood donation for 21 days or until the scab has separated.
